::: {.why}
The result is one line of calculus and the interesting part is what it optimises, which is not what most people who cite it think it is.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Derive the Kelly fraction by maximising expected log wealth and state what objective that corresponds to.
- Say what full Kelly does to the distribution of terminal wealth, in terms of median against mean.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Derive it: maximise the expected log of one plus the fraction times the payoff, for a binary bet. Then say what the log objective means, which is maximising the almost-sure long-run growth rate rather than expected wealth, and note that maximising expected wealth would tell you to bet everything.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Simulate to see the shape: 10,000 paths of 1,000 bets at your Kelly fraction, at half of it, and at twice it. Plot the distribution of terminal log wealth for each, and report the median and the fraction of paths that lost money. The double-Kelly case is the one worth staring at.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Write down the result you will use: growth rate is zero at twice Kelly, which means the penalty for overbetting is severe and asymmetric.
:::
:::
